title: VAT, SSCL reliefs cost Rs. 636 b in 2025 | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:00
-     - 173

Value Added Tax (VAT) and Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) reliefs cost Sri Lanka Rs. 636 billion in 2025, and the Finance Ministry warned that the true figure is likely to be higher.

The Ministry’s Tax Expenditure Statement 2025/2026 shows VAT reliefs rose 25.8% to Rs. 419 billion in 2025 from Rs. 333 billion in 2024, an increase of Rs. 86 billion. SSCL reliefs amounted to Rs. 216 billion. VAT is charged at a standard rate of 18%, while SSCL is levied at 2.5% of liable turnover.

Non-Board of Investment (BOI) companies, excluding Strategic Development Projects (SDPs) and Port City projects, accounted for Rs. 391 billion of VAT relief and Rs. 200 billion of SSCL relief. Among them, the wholesale and retail sector received Rs. 188 billion in VAT relief and Rs. 54 billion in SSCL relief. 

Electricity and gas received Rs. 65 billion in VAT relief, other manufacturing activities Rs. 47 billion, and construction Rs. 38 billion. In SSCL, other manufacturing activities received Rs. 20 billion, textiles and garments Rs. 16 billion and transport Rs. 14 billion.

The trend continued into 2026. VAT reliefs reached Rs. 243 billion in the first half, 17.2% higher than the Rs. 207 billion recorded a year earlier, while SSCL reliefs amounted to Rs. 135 billion. Wholesale and retail again led VAT reliefs for non-BOI companies at Rs. 113 billion, followed by electricity and gas at Rs. 36 billion. Construction fell to Rs. 8.2 billion.

The statement disclosed one new VAT relief: an exemption on liquid milk and yoghurt made from locally produced fresh milk, effective from 11 April 2025.

However, the Ministry said the estimates understate the full cost. “The VAT and SSCL estimates are calculated based exclusively on tax returns filed by registered taxpayers. This represents a major limitation, as it fails to capture the true size of the country’s actual or potential economic supply,” the statement said.

Measuring the full cost would require national supply and use tables and detailed consumption data, which the Ministry said are not fully available. “Because we cannot measure the gap between total potential economic supply and what is formally reported, these VAT and SSCL expenditure figures should be viewed as a conservative minimum rather than the absolute total of foregone revenue,” it said.

The statement’s list of individual VAT and SSCL exemptions, which covers items ranging from wheat flour, infant milk powder and pharmaceuticals to electricity, tea and tourism services, carries no cost estimates for 2024, 2025 or the first half of 2026. The only items with figures are two Port City VAT reliefs, both for 2024 only. “Where a provision is identified as a potential tax expenditure but cannot be reliably quantified, it is disclosed separately rather than presented with an unsupported estimate,” the Ministry said.

title: Customs duty reliefs cost Rs. 144 b in 2025 | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:30
-     - 83

Customs Import Duty (CID) reliefs rose 4.4% to Rs. 144 billion in 2025 from Rs. 138 billion in 2024, driven by duty waivers on fuel imports, the Finance Ministry’s Tax Expenditure Statement (TES) 2025/2026 showed.

Waivers granted for general purposes and special projects under Section 19A of the Customs Ordinance accounted for Rs. 131 billion, or 91% of the total. The statement describes these waivers as covering consumer goods, to improve living standards, and special infrastructure projects that contribute to economic development.

They rose by Rs. 7.1 billion, or 5.7%, from Rs. 124 billion in 2024, as combined petrol and diesel imports increased 5.4% to 2.51 million metric tons from 2.38 million metric tons.

Part of the increase reflects a broader count. “The CID expenditure related to Section 19A general waivers was limited to diesel and wheat grain products in the TES 2024/2025. However, the CID expenditure related to Section 19A general waivers was extended to cover products including petrol and bamboo sticks, together with other products identified in the Customs database, in the TES 2025/2026,” the Ministry said, adding that the 2024 data were revised accordingly.

Exemptions on ingredients other than maize, lentils, and rice used to manufacture animal feed were the second-largest item at Rs. 7.8 billion, or 5.4% of the total, down from Rs. 9.2 billion in 2024. Exemptions on machinery and equipment for the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) and its subsidiaries fell to Rs. 1.1 billion from Rs. 1.8 billion.

Medicine-related exemptions rose to Rs. 1.4 billion from Rs. 1.3 billion. These comprised Rs. 870 million on products registered with the National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA), Rs. 495 million on raw and packing materials for pharmaceutical manufacturing, and Rs. 12 million on raw materials for Ayurvedic medicine. Materials for agricultural purposes received Rs. 394 million in relief and raw materials for sanitary napkins Rs. 56 million, down from Rs. 78 million.

In the first half of 2026, CID reliefs amounted to Rs. 74 billion. Section 19A waivers accounted for Rs. 67 billion, or 89.8%, followed by animal feed ingredients at Rs. 4.9 billion, or 6.6%. CEB-related exemptions fell to Rs. 179 million, or 0.24%.

The estimates are measured against the standard tariff applied to all imports on a Most Favoured Nation basis. That standard excludes concessions under Board of Investment (BOI) agreements, Free Trade Agreements, and project-specific exemptions. “Although the tariff structure may contain commonly applied rates, the applicable rate varies according to the commodity and tariff classification,” the Ministry said.

Several Customs concessions are treated as part of the normal structure of the tax and are therefore excluded from the estimates. These include reduced tariffs under Free Trade Agreements, duty-free imports into bonded warehouses for re-export, materials imported for export processing under the Temporary Import for Export Processing (TIEP) and Investor Facilitation Centre (INFAC) schemes, and imports by diplomatic missions. “Not every provision that reduces tax relative to a theoretical or simplified tax base constitutes a tax expenditure,” the Ministry said.

title: Wake-up call to economists in stagnant economy: Take market case to public | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:28
-     - 98

World Bank Lead Economist 

Dr. Harsha Aturupane 

– Pic by Shehan Gunasekara

Sri Lanka’s economists understand growth, markets and the role of the State better than ever, but the public they must persuade still backs a market-stifling model, and closing that gap is now the profession’s main task, World Bank Lead Economist Dr. Harsha Aturupane said.

The distinction matters because in a democracy, economic policy can only go as far as voters will allow. Economists can diagnose problems and design solutions, but reforms that lack public consent tend to be diluted, delayed or reversed at the next election. 

Sri Lanka’s recovery since the 2022 crisis rests on an IMF-backed program of higher taxes, cost-reflective energy pricing, State-owned enterprise restructuring and an independent Central Bank, and every one of these measures is politically contested. 

Dr. Aturupane’s argument moves the binding constraint on growth from technical knowledge to public persuasion. That makes the durability of reform as much a question of whether economists can win the public argument as of whether their prescriptions are right.

Delivering the keynote address at the Sri Lanka Economic Association (SLEA) Annual International Conference last Saturday, Dr. Aturupane told the gathering that this gap explains why the country remains stuck.

“Our country, I often think, is the last country fighting the Cold War, the economics of the Cold War, on the losing side,” he said.

He said the gap has not always run this way. In the early 1970s, which he called the worst period in Sri Lanka’s economic history up to then for stifling markets, people queued for hours for a quarter pound of bread and went home hungry. Many economists of that era, academics among them, strongly backed those policies. It was the public that broke with them.

“1977 is when our population rejected that economic model and brought in a model more concerned with what we know of the dynamism of markets and the importance of a liberalised economy,” Dr. Aturupane said.

That position has now reversed. He said economists in academia, policymaking, the private sector and research have a good grasp of growth and of the roles of the State and markets. The public, however, still works with a model in which markets are to be stifled, for reasons he described as emotional or imaginary.

He said recent history shows the problem is not a lack of economic knowledge. From 2008, economists warned against borrowing on private international markets at very high interest rates to fund activities that did not earn enough foreign exchange to repay the loans. The Central Bank and academics also warned the Government that it could not control the inflation rate, the interest rate and the exchange rate at the same time. Governments went ahead regardless.

“We would encounter economic disaster, and we did. It was just a case of when, not if,” Dr. Aturupane said.

He added that the 2019 tax cuts and the deficit financing that followed were wrongly presented as Keynesian demand stimulus. That tool is meant for an economy in recession that is producing below its capacity. It does not expand the capacity of a developing economy.

The blind spot in public debate, he argued, is State failure. Markets can produce very unequal outcomes, and the case for State intervention in the interest of social justice is deeply rooted in the Sri Lankan psyche and drives voter behaviour. 

The costs of State failure are far less understood: short-sighted policymaking, administrative and enforcement costs, loss-making State-owned enterprises funded by taxpayers, power imbalances between the State and the population, and rent-seeking, ‘popularly known as corruption’. He urged university economists to give it more emphasis in their courses.

“State failure is more dangerous and more damaging than market failure. The State can drive an entire population into poverty. The State is much more powerful than any one agency in the market,” he said.

His example was 2022, when the exchange rate collapsed from Rs. 201 to Rs. 360.

Dr. Aturupane said the same history shows what market-friendly institutions can achieve. The 1833 Colebrooke-Cameron report drew on the classical economics of Adam Smith, Jeremy Bentham and David Ricardo, and it laid the framework for the plantation economy. He said international data sets show Sri Lanka had the highest per capita income in Asia, above Japan’s, from about the 1830s to about the 1920s. Market-stifling policies later cost the country its competitiveness, and market-oriented economies overtook it.

The cost is still visible. Sri Lanka scores well below what its per capita income would predict on the 2025 Knowledge Economy Index, which rests on human capital, information and communications technology, innovation, financial foundations and the quality of institutions. It also underperforms on the gross enrolment rate in tertiary education and on innovation and technology indices.

Dr. Aturupane also took on the term ‘neoliberalism’, which he said is a political label rather than a school of economic thought. He pointed to the liberalisation wave led by J.R. Jayewardene in 1977, Deng Xiaoping in China, Margaret Thatcher in Britain from 1979 and Ronald Reagan in the US from 1980. He said the globalisation that followed generated wealth on a scale never seen before in human history. 

“When people argue against neoliberalism, I take the position that the empirical evidence is fully in favour of a democratic political system and a modern market economy. I hope the economics profession can take this message out in a persuasive way,” he said.

title: World Bank Group expands local currency financing in Asia with first Sri Lankan rupee facility | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:25
-     - 129

The World Bank Group is expanding access to longer-term Sri Lankan rupee financing to help businesses reduce foreign exchange risk and enabling new private investment in renewable energy and infrastructure.

 In a first of its kind transaction in Asia, the World Bank Group Treasury has arranged a six-year Sri Lankan rupee (LKR) borrowing line between the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group focused on the private sector, and HSBC Sri Lanka. The fixed-rate facility, equivalent to $ 5 million, is the IFC’s first borrowing line in Sri Lanka.

The facility is already helping mobilise longer-term financing for renewable energy in Sri Lanka. Combined with additional local currency funding arranged by the World Bank Group Treasury, it supports the IFC’s $ 10 million, 10-year rupee-denominated loan to one of Sri Lanka’s largest renewable energy companies. The investment is the IFC’s longest-tenor rupee loan to date, its first rupee-denominated infrastructure loan, and its first infrastructure investment in Sri Lanka since the country’s recent economic crisis.

 By raising rupees locally, the World Bank Group can lend in the currency businesses earn in, reducing their exposure to exchange-rate risks. Building on this first facility, the World Bank Group aims to expand long-term local currency financing in Sri Lanka to support private investment and growth.

World Bank Group Treasury Director Client Solutions and Structuring Keshav Gaur said:  “Access to long-term local currency financing can help businesses invest, grow and create jobs without taking on foreign exchange risk they may not be able to manage. This first borrowing line in Asia expands the financing solutions we can bring to emerging markets, helping channel private investment to sectors that can drive growth and economic opportunity.”

 

The transaction forms part of HSBC’s broader partnership with the World Bank Group in Sri Lanka and across HSBC’s global network. HSBC participates in the World Bank Group’s Private Sector Investment Lab to identify new avenues for public-private collaboration and mobilise private capital to support sustainable development.

 

HSBC Sri Lanka CEO Mark Surgenor said: “We are proud to support this milestone partnership with IFC, which expands access to longer-term Sri Lankan rupee financing for companies and helps them manage foreign-exchange risk. By combining HSBC’s local expertise and global capabilities with the IFC’s development mandate, we look forward to exploring further practical solutions that support Sri Lankan businesses and the country’s longer-term priorities.”

The Sri Lanka facility builds on borrowing lines established by the IFC and Citi in Kenya in 2024 and South Africa in 2026. Over the past decade, IFC has committed more than $ 33 billion in local currency financing across 71 currencies, helping businesses access longer-term financing in markets where it is often limited.

title: Public consultation converges on 4-5% inflation target: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:24
-     - 89

A public consultation on Sri Lanka’s inflation target drew about 100 responses that converged around 4-5%, Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) officials told Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) recently. They presented the response as support for keeping the target at 5%, at a time when inflation is running well above the band.

The consultation results matter because they back the CBSL’s central argument for not lowering the target: an economy with few fiscal buffers and heavy exposure to supply shocks cannot credibly commit to a lower target.

That argument also shifts part of the burden of price stability onto fiscal policy, a point Committee members pressed the officials on.

The officials said the online consultation was one of two inputs into the review, along with a detailed analysis by the CBSL’s Economic Research Department of what other countries do and which target suits Sri Lanka. That analysis was shared with the Ministry of Finance, which questioned the CBSL at several fora before the target was agreed. Responding to the view that 100 responses was too few, the officials noted that similar reviews in larger economies drew fewer, citing about 70 in India.

“There was convergence around 4-5%. It was not as if there was a majority for 2% and a majority for 7%, but some views were expressed that a more appropriate target for Sri Lanka would be something like 7%. So it was not one-sided,” a CBSL official told CoPF Chaired by SJB MP Dr. Harsha de Silva.

The Monetary Policy Framework Agreement signed by the Governor and the Minister of Finance on 1 October, 2026 and published in the Gazette retains the 5% target, the accountability margin of ±2 percentage points and headline inflation measured by the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI) as the target variable. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act requires the target to be reviewed at least every three years. The first agreement was signed in October 2023.

The officials said the main consideration was that the structure of the economy had not changed significantly over the three years, and in particular its ability to withstand shocks. They pointed to the Middle East conflict, which pushed inflation from 2.2% in March to 8%, an acceleration of more than 5 percentage points within a few months. Most countries, mainly advanced economies, have fiscal buffers that let them absorb such shocks on the Government’s balance sheet and soften the impact on the economy.

“When there is a large supply shock and there is fiscal space to respond, the impact of the shock can be mitigated. The main instrument to deal with a supply shock is fiscal policy,” an official said.

Committee members questioned whether, since supply-side shocks beyond the reach of interest rates were driving the misses, responsibility for price stability should be shared rather than placed on the CBSL alone. They said the headline story would always be that the Central Bank missed its target, while the fiscal side went undiscussed. The officials replied that the Ministry of Finance’s role is limited to agreeing the target. “The Government is not involved in monetary policy decisions,” an official said.

They said accountability works through a coordination council of the Government and the Central Bank, which meets once every three months to discuss the implications of monetary policy for inflation and fiscal policy, and through the CBSL’s legal obligation to explain deviations to Parliament, the Government, markets and the public, and to recommend Government action on the supply side. As an example, the officials said a subsidy had been allocated this year mainly for that reason, after the CBSL alerted the Government through the council.

On the choice of headline over core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, the officials said core inflation means little to the public. “Headline inflation is what people feel. It is actual inflation,” an official said. Of the 20-25 countries in the CBSL’s sample, only one targets core inflation.

The consultation outcome comes as inflation moves further from target. On 20 November, 2026 the Monetary Policy Board raised the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 25 basis points to 9%, and raised the Statutory Reserve Ratio by one percentage point to 3%, effective from the reserve maintenance period beginning 9 December, 2026. Most economists polled by Bloomberg had expected no change. The CBSL last tightened in May, with a 100 basis point increase to 8.75%.

CCPI headline inflation rose to 8.3% in October from 8% in September, its fourth straight month above the band, while core inflation rose to 5.6% from 5.4%. The Board pointed to the prolonged Middle East conflict and the high global energy prices it has caused. 

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said headline inflation could reach about 9% by the end of November and stay near that level in the short term. When the CBSL raised rates in May, its projections showed inflation peaking at 7-8% before easing. The CBSL’s projections from the September round assume that the effects of the Middle East tensions will gradually fade.

title: Sri Lanka must prepare exporters for EU green rules and shifting global supply chains: Expert | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:23
-     - 75

ODI Global Principal Research Fellow Jodie Keane 

— Pic by Lasantha Kumara

By Charumini de Silva

Sri Lanka must urgently strengthen its trade governance, upgrade supply chain capabilities, and prepare exporters for tightening environmental regulations, as geopolitical realignments reshape global trade and investment flows, ODI Global Principal Research Fellow Jodie Keane said.

Addressing an Asian Development Bank (ADB) knowledge event, organised in partnership with the Department of External Resources of the Finance Ministry yesterday, she warned that emerging climate-related trade measures could increase compliance costs and undermine the competitiveness of Sri Lankan producers, unless targeted support mechanisms are introduced.

Highlighting what she termed a growing ‘green squeeze’ on Sri Lanka, Keane said the country’s continued reliance on commodities within its export basket exposed producers to new regulatory risks, particularly in rubber and apparel.

Her analysis indicated that Sri Lanka’s rubber production could be adversely affected by emerging trade-related climate measures, while apparel manufacturers would also need to adjust to new requirements, including the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). 

“Trade policy could no longer be approached through broad-based reforms alone, but needed to address the specific vulnerabilities and opportunities within individual sectors and value chains,” she stressed.

Keane also pointed to the need for stronger partnerships to help producers adapt to climate change, noting that while new regulatory requirements were emerging, comparable trade-related partnerships providing financing and adaptation support remain limited.

Against an increasingly fragmented global trading environment, she said the retreat from traditional globalisation in parts of the developed world was occurring alongside growing optimism in developing economies, where trade reforms and regional integration were creating new opportunities.

“The expansion of South-South trade, services, and digitally delivered services was reshaping international commerce, offering smaller economies and enterprises new avenues to participate in global value chains,” she added.

She noted that despite mounting pressure on the multilateral trading system, around 72% of global merchandise trade continued to take place under World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules, underscoring the continued relevance of the rules-based trading framework.

For Sri Lanka, she said the evolving trade architecture also presented opportunities arising from supply chain diversification, particularly as companies and countries sought to reduce their dependence on China and build more resilient manufacturing networks.

Keane highlighted the EU’s proposed ‘Made in Europe’ initiative, which seeks to increase the bloc’s share of global manufacturing from around 14% to 20%, as a development Sri Lanka should monitor closely.

The implications of the EU’s emerging trade arrangements with India, and potential spillovers to countries connected to India through geography and trade agreements, could also influence future supply chain opportunities.

“Sri Lanka should position itself to benefit from these shifts through stronger regional partnerships and a more strategic approach to trade and investment,” she added. 

Another significant opportunity she outlined was in the development of maritime economic corridors, mainly because decarbonisation requirements reshape shipping and port infrastructure. Increasing carbon-related costs in maritime transport were expected to accelerate demand for sustainable fuels, greener ports, and more resilient logistics infrastructure.

Keane advocated moving beyond infrastructure projects towards integrated regional economic corridors, supported by concessional finance, blended investment, technical assistance, and private capital.

However, she cautioned that physical connectivity needed to be matched by digital and institutional improvements. While Sri Lankan firms already demonstrated relatively high e-commerce adoption, weaknesses in Customs and payment procedures continued to constrain their ability to fully capitalise on digital trade opportunities.

She asserted the need to strengthen digital infrastructure, streamline Customs processes, and improve support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to participate more effectively in cross-border commerce.

Keane also called for stronger institutional capacity, monitoring and evaluation frameworks, and policies that balance economic efficiency with longer-term economic security, employment, and livelihoods. 

“The benefits of international trade can be tremendous and positive, but we also need to be vigilant regarding the impacts of trade on different groups of people within specific sectors,” she said, stressing that adjustment costs should not fall disproportionately on vulnerable groups.

She said the next phase of global trade would be shaped less by conventional Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and more by strategic partnerships built around shared resilience, sustainability, and investment priorities.

title: ADB urges deeper trade reforms as Sri Lanka’s global value chain integration lags peers | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:22
-     - 59

Asian Development Bank (ADB) Country Director Shannon Cowlin yesterday said Sri Lanka must accelerate trade reforms and deepen integration into global production networks to sustain its economic recovery, with exports, investments and productivity emerging as critical drivers of the next phase of growth.

Speaking at an ADB Serendipity Knowledge Program’s trade reform forum, organised in partnership with the Department of External Resources of the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry, he said Sri Lanka had made significant progress in restoring macroeconomic stability, but this alone would not deliver sustained growth and prosperity.

Highlighting the country’s weak integration into global value chains, Cowlin said such trade accounted for 31% of Sri Lanka’s gross trade in 2024, compared with 63% in Vietnam.

She pointed to the longstanding export underperformance to the concentration of merchandise exports in a few traditional sectors, low foreign direct investment (FDI), high import protection, policy uncertainty and regulatory and institutional constraints that have discouraged diversification and investment in competitive industries.

“The changing global trading environment has made reforms more urgent,” she said, warning that Sri Lankan exporters risk losing competitiveness as other economies secure preferential market access through comprehensive trade agreements. 

Cowlin cited India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), as an example of evolving competitive landscape.

Welcoming Sri Lanka’s efforts to pursue accession to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), she cautioned that improved market access alone would not automatically translate into higher exports.

“Trade integration must be supported by domestic reforms that lower trading costs, improve the investment climate and enable businesses to innovate, diversify and raise productivity,” she stressed.

The Country Manage also noted that the National Export Development Plan (NEDP) 2026-2030 as an important framework for export diversification, stating that ADB had supported its development through its trade, investment and industry development program and was providing technical assistance for Sri Lanka’s RCEP accession process.

She asserted that the success of these initiatives would ultimately depend on implementation and their ability to deliver measurable improvements in export performance, investment and productivity.

title: Digital Trust Alliance launches open dashboard tracking digital spending in Budget 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:07
-     - 9

The Digital Trust Alliance (DTA) has launched “Budget 2027: What’s for Digital”, a free, publicly accessible dashboard at budget.digitaltrust.lk that sets out how Sri Lanka’s draft Budget 2027 allocates funds to digital government, cybersecurity, data protection, digital skills and related areas, and how these allocations compare with Budget 2026.

Budget analyses published each year by professional services firms and policy think tanks provide valuable insight into revenue, expenditure and the fiscal outlook. The DTA dashboard is intended to complement this work by focusing on the digital and digital trust dimensions of public spending. Digital allocations are spread across the Appropriation Bill, the volumes of Detailed Budget Estimates, the medium-term public investment plan and the Budget Speech; the dashboard brings these lines together in one place and identifies Rs. 52.5 billion in digital spending in the 2027 draft.

Key observations

Ministry of Digital Economy: Rs. 26,000 million in 2027, up 62.5% from Rs. 16,000 million in 2026.

Digital government (DigiGov-SL): Rs. 9,486 million in 2027, up from a revised Rs. 702 million in 2026, within an estimated total programme cost of Rs. 43,859 million to 2030. Of the 2027 allocation, Rs. 7,026 million is foreign loan financing.

Digital identity (SLUDI): Rs. 1,500 million in 2027, following a revision of the 2026 allocation from Rs. 2,110 million to Rs. 910 million.

Cybersecurity: projects under Sri Lanka CERT receive Rs. 590 million (2026: Rs. 600 million), while its institutional grant rises from Rs. 375 million to Rs. 470 million. New Ministry of Defence lines for cyber infrastructure, a digital forensic laboratory and a cyber range total Rs. 1,053 million.

Data protection: the Data Protection Authority receives Rs. 195 million (2026: Rs. 174 million), ahead of the operative provisions of the Personal Data Protection Act taking effect on 1 January 2027.

Skills and industry: ICT Hubs for secondary schools rise from Rs. 575 million to Rs 2,500 million, while the Digital Industry Development line, which supports upskilling and start-up accelerators, is allocated Rs. 380 million, down 49.3% from Rs. 750 million.

Oversight: the National Audit Office, the Bribery Commission and the National Procurement Commission together hold under Rs. 45 million for software in 2027.

Delivery: by August 2026, 25.4% of the 2026 capital budget had been spent across government. Budget 2026 commitments on GovPay and VAT on foreign digital services have been delivered.

Legislation: Budget Speech 2027 expects the Digital Economy Bill, which establishes the Digital Economy Authority, to be passed in the first quarter of 2027. The Cyber Security Bill is with the Attorney General.

Digital Trust Alliance President Lakmal Embuldeniya said: “Each year, professional firms and think tanks provide valuable commentary on the Budget, and we aim to add a digital trust lens to that conversation. Budget 2027 makes a meaningful investment in digital public infrastructure. The dashboard allows anyone to see where that money is allocated, how it compares with last year, and whether investment in digital platforms is matched by investment in cybersecurity, data protection and oversight. It is a living tool that we will continue to improve, and we invite citizens to help shape it through their comments. We also hope it gives investors, both local and foreign, a clear and transparent view of Sri Lanka’s digital priorities.”

Methodology and transparency

Every figure on the dashboard is tagged to the page of the official document from which it is drawn, and figures calculated by the DTA, as well as analytical observations, are labelled separately. The DTA used generative AI tools to convert the budget documents and assist with the analysis; each figure can be checked against its original source page. Sources include the Appropriation Bill 2027, the Draft Detailed Budget Estimates 2027, the medium-term public investment plan for 2027 to 2029, the Treasury’s 2027 budget economic and fiscal position report, and the Budget Speeches for 2026 and 2027.

All 2027 figures are drafts and may change before Parliament’s final vote on 14 December 2026. The DTA will update the dashboard to reflect the approved Budget.

The DTA is a Sri Lanka-based alliance that brings together professionals and organisations to advance cybersecurity, information security, governance, risk, compliance and privacy. Through knowledge-sharing, capacity building and evidence-based dialogue with policymakers, industry and civil society, the DTA works to strengthen trust in Sri Lanka’s digital economy and digital public services.

title: GRI Executive Director Ananda Caldera receives PRISL Lifetime Achievement Award | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:06
-     - 14

Ananda Caldera

The Plastics & Rubber Institute of Sri Lanka (PRISL) on 17 November presented its Lifetime Achievement Award to Global Rubber Industries (GRI) Executive Director Ananda Caldera. 

A former President of the Institute, Caldera is only the fourth person to receive the distinction, which recognises more than four decades of service to Sri Lanka’s rubber industry.

A qualified engineer, Caldera served as Director of Manufacturing before joining GRI. During that time, he established a custom rubber-mixing facility and introduced hot-process retreading for off-the-road tires in Sri Lanka, giving these heavy-duty tires a second working life.

Since joining GRI on 1 January 2012, Caldera has helped lead the expansion of its specialty tire manufacturing operations in Sri Lanka. Under his guidance, GRI has strengthened its international presence, bringing Sri Lankan-made agricultural and industrial tires to farms and workplaces around the world and showcasing the expertise of the country’s rubber manufacturers.

Caldera has brought the voice of Sri Lanka’s rubber manufacturers and exporters to national industry discussions. He chaired the Sri Lanka Association of Manufacturers and Exporters of Rubber Products and the Ministry of Industries’ Rubber Sector Advisory Board. In 2018, the President of Sri Lanka appointed him to the Industrialisation Commission. Today, he serves on advisory committees of the Export Development Board, the Ministry of Industry and the University of Moratuwa, where he earned his MBA in Management of Technology.

At GRI, we are proud to work alongside Caldera and to be among the generations of rubber professionals who have learned from him. For those of us who continue to benefit from his guidance, it means a great deal to see the Institute he once led honor his contribution to Sri Lanka’s rubber industry and its people.

Volfpack SLTC team TRACE

Sri Lanka has produced its first supercapacitors, the fast response energy storage that factories, data centres and power grids increasingly rely on. Volfpack Energy, a Sri Lankan deep tech startup working with Sri Lanka Technology Campus (SLTC), has made the cells in its laboratory and is now building towards commercial production. Apparel manufacturers and IT infrastructure companies are already evaluating the technology.

The timing reflects a shift in what industry needs from the grid. Sri Lanka now has more than 3,000 MW of solar capacity, yet the grid was designed for one way power flow and has limited storage to absorb sudden swings in supply. October’s nationwide blackout and an 18% tariff increase this year have made power quality a board level concern. For manufacturers the risk is immediate, because a voltage dip lasting less than a second can stop an entire production line.

CVolfpack Energy CEO and Co-founder harlie Karunaratne said: “It’s not just about generating more electricity. It’s about managing electricity better.” 

Supercapacitors store charge on the surface of porous carbon rather than through a chemical reaction, so they charge and release power in seconds. Volfpack’s graphene enhanced cells are rated for up to one million cycles, compared with 5,000 to 6,000 for the batteries most factories use today. The cells deliver power densities of up to 18 kW/kg, and Volfpack is developing stackable 10 kW energy storage modules that scale to 100 kW and beyond. Installed alongside batteries, they are designed to absorb the sudden bursts of demand from heavy machinery and servers that wear batteries down, which would allow battery systems to offer warranties of up to 10 years. The same capability could smooth rapid swings in solar output before they reach the grid. The cells are built for bursts lasting seconds and do not replace long duration backup power.

Alongside supercapacitors, Volfpack is developing 10C batteries for applications that need more energy, with a target duration of up to 15 minutes. Both technologies share a common manufacturing platform.

Over the past four years, Volfpack’s team of young scientists and engineers has manufactured more than 5,000 cells and developed its own electrode and electrolyte formulations. The company is based at TRACE Expert City, where it works with SLTC at the SLTC Innovation & Industry Collaboration Hub.

The development also moves Sri Lanka further up a value chain in which it already competes globally. The country is one of the world’s ten largest exporters of activated carbon, most of it made from coconut shells, a preferred material for supercapacitor electrodes. Volfpack aims to turn this local resource into finished energy storage products made in Sri Lanka. No other company in the country has made supercapacitors from these resources at this power level.

SLTC students work alongside Volfpack’s engineers on device design, production, automation, testing and quality control.

SLTC Electrical Engineering Head Dr. Nicoloy Gurusinghe said: “Developing energy-storage technology is only the beginning. The real challenge is making it work reliably in real-world applications. This collaboration gives students hands-on experience in testing, product development and manufacturing, helping them understand how engineering something people can actually use becomes.” 

SLTC Applied Electronics Head Dr. Chamith Chandrarathna said: “Engineering education becomes more meaningful when students can apply what they learn to real problems. Working with Volfpack exposes them to the pace of product development, the importance of testing and iteration, and the challenges of building technology that works beyond the classroom.”

Volfpack’s first manufacturing milestone is one million cells a year, with India and the wider South Asian region as its first export markets. “The goal is to prove that we can manufacture consistently, at a competitive cost, while building products that solve problems customers are actually willing to pay for,” said Karunaratne.

 Volfpack is inviting manufacturers and data centre operators to pilot the technology.

The development builds on the European Union’s (EU) recognition of Ceylon Cinnamon as a GI on 2 February 2022, making it the first Sri Lankan product to secure GI registration in the EU. The national certification is expected to reinforce protection of the product’s geographical identity, distinguish authentic Sri Lankan cinnamon from substitutes and support its positioning in premium international markets.

Sri Lanka earned around $ 250 million from cinnamon exports in 2025, with the industry now targeting expansion into a $ 1 billion export sector by around 2030, supported by GI recognition, improved quality, value addition and wider market access.

The GI designation is intended to strengthen Sri Lanka’s competitive advantage by ensuring that products marketed as Ceylon Cinnamon meet specified quality and geographical origin requirements. It is also expected to support higher prices, export diversification, increased production and employment across the value chain.

A key component of the certification framework is the Association for Ceylon Cinnamon Protected Geographical Indication (ACCPGI), established to represent stakeholders across the industry. The association is responsible for an internal control mechanism to monitor compliance with the GI specification. Growers, processors, traders, exporters and other supply-chain participants must register with the association to export Ceylon Cinnamon to the EU under the protected name.

The achievement follows sustained efforts by the EDB, with technical assistance from the EU Delegation to Sri Lanka, the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) and the World Trade Organization (WTO). Financial support was provided by the Netherlands-based Common Fund for Commodities, while the International Finance Corporation (IFC) supported promotional activities and industry training.

The EDB also worked with the Trade and Foreign Affairs Ministries, Department of Commerce, Department of Export Agriculture, NIPO, the Spice Council and the Spices and Allied Products Producers' and Traders' Association (SAPPTA) to secure the recognition, despite objections raised by competing countries before the European Commission.

Established with effect from 1 September 2023, the Cinnamon Development Department is also tasked with elevating cinnamon from a relatively minor export crop into a major commercial plantation industry by improving production, quality and export performance.

title: India is region’s economic giant. Will Sri Lanka remain a neighbour or become a partner? | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:28
-     - 19

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake during the former's visit to Sri Lanka in April 2025

More than 2,300 years of civilisational exchange have bound India and Sri Lanka together. Today, India's economic ascent presents another historic opportunity. But the greatest threat to 

Sri Lankan sovereignty may not be India's growing influence; it may be Lanka's failure to develop the economic strength necessary to negotiate that influence

More than 2,300 years ago, an encounter between Arahat Mahinda and King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale transformed Sri Lankan civilisation. According to Buddhist chronicles, Arahat Mahinda arrived during Emperor Ashoka’s reign, introducing a philosophical tradition that profoundly influenced the island’s religious, intellectual and political institutions. Buddhism shaped the monasteries of Anuradhapura, the sacred Sri Maha Bodhi and traditions central to Sri Lankan identity. Yet this civilisational relationship extended beyond Buddhism. Hindu devales became incorporated into Buddhist religious complexes, while deities including Vishnu, Kataragama and Pattini acquired distinctive positions within Sinhala Buddhist worship. At Kandy, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and neighbouring devales embody centuries of religious interaction. These influences were not merely imported; they became inseparable from Sri Lanka’s cultural identity.

There is a political lesson in this history. Sri Lanka absorbed external influences without becoming an extension of India, yet contemporary foreign policy frequently approaches economic proximity through anxieties about sovereignty and unequal power. That anxiety now confronts an extraordinary transformation. India has emerged as an economic giant whose industrial expansion is reshaping South Asia, while Sri Lanka continues rebuilding after sovereign default. The question is no longer whether India will influence Sri Lanka’s economic future, but whether Sri Lanka possesses the productive strength to shape that relationship rather than remain vulnerable to it.

History must inform foreign policy, not imprison it

India–Sri Lanka relations cannot be reduced to civilisational friendship. India’s involvement in Sri Lanka’s ethnic conflict, the Indo-Lanka Accord of 1987, the Indian Peace Keeping Force and unresolved Tamil political grievances have left enduring consequences. Fisheries disputes demonstrate that geographical proximity can generate conflicting interests. These experiences warrant scrutiny, but allowing historical grievances to determine the limits of economic cooperation risks transforming foreign policy into a permanent negotiation with the past.

India is not Tamil Nadu alone. Its economic geography encompasses Maharashtra’s industrial centres, Gujarat’s manufacturing networks, Karnataka’s technology ecosystem and Telangana’s pharmaceutical industries. A mature foreign policy must distinguish legitimate concerns about interference from opportunities for industrial development. Sri Lanka’s cultural history demonstrates that exchange and autonomy have long coexisted; modern economic diplomacy requires comparable confidence, accompanied by stronger institutional safeguards.

India’s rise was constructed, not inherited

India’s economic prominence is measurable. The International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 projections place its nominal gross domestic product at approximately $4.06 trillion, with real growth projected at 7%. Measured through purchasing power parity, its economy approaches $19.2 trillion, accounting for approximately 8.6% of global output. India is therefore not merely South Asia’s dominant economy but an increasingly consequential centre of international economic activity.


Its transformation reflects decades of reform, entrepreneurship, technological development and integration into global markets. Liberalisation introduced in 1991 reduced restrictions and enabled domestic enterprises to expand internationally. Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and Wipro became globally competitive technology businesses, while Tata Motors, Mahindra and Bharat Forge developed manufacturing capabilities extending beyond India’s borders. Tata’s acquisition of Jaguar Land Rover in 2008 demonstrated an important transition: Indian corporations were no longer merely participating in global production networks but acquiring technological capabilities, established brands and international distribution systems.

India’s growth remains uneven, with informal employment and regional inequalities exposing the limitations of aggregate expansion. Nevertheless, the comparison with Sri Lanka is uncomfortable. The island liberalised its economy in 1977, fourteen years before India’s major reforms, but failed to consolidate that advantage into sustained industrial competitiveness. Regulatory uncertainty, political instability and repeated policy reversals constrained diversification. India’s rise demonstrates what institutional continuity and industrial capability can achieve; Sri Lanka’s experience exposes the consequences of repeatedly failing to develop them.

Sri Lanka must stop merely trading with India and start producing with it

Sri Lanka’s bilateral trade relationship reveals the limitations of an economic strategy centred predominantly on market access. Department of Commerce figures show exports to India reached approximately $1.04 billion in 2025, while imports amounted to $4.33 billion, producing a merchandise trade deficit of approximately $3.3 billion. A trade deficit does not inherently indicate economic weakness, particularly when imported machinery and intermediate goods support production. The more consequential question is whether trade creates skilled employment, technological capabilities and competitive industries.

The India–Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement offers a revealing historical lesson. Following its implementation in 2000, exports expanded rapidly, but much of the initial growth became concentrated in vanaspati and copper. Research by the Institute of Policy Studies found that these products accounted for more than half of exports to India by 2005. Their competitiveness depended substantially on tariff advantages rather than durable industrial strengths. Following Indian restrictions and regulatory changes, vanaspati exports ceased, while copper exports fell from approximately $145 million in 2005 to $13 million in 2008. The episode exposed the difference between temporary market access and sustainable industrial capability.

A contrasting example exists in the CEAT–Kelani partnership. Established through an alliance in 1999, the venture combined Indian industrial expertise with Sri Lankan manufacturing assets, subsequently expanding production capacity and technological capabilities. CEAT’s documented investments included radial-tyre manufacturing and truck-and-bus tyre production. Unlike businesses dependent principally on temporary tariff advantages, manufacturing partnerships require equipment, skilled labour, technical knowledge and continuing investment.

The opportunity extends further. India’s automotive-component industry generated approximately $85.9 billion in turnover during 2025–26, including $24 billion in exports, according to the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association of India. Sri Lanka already manufactures rubber products, electrical assemblies and specialised automotive components. Rather than attempting to replicate India’s industrial scale, its enterprises could become qualified suppliers within Indian manufacturing networks through certification, technological partnerships and efficient logistics.

CEAT–Kelani demonstrates industrial feasibility, not evidence of contracts Sri Lanka has already lost. The failure lies in the absence of a sufficiently sustained national strategy to replicate such capabilities across sectors. Bilateral cooperation should ultimately be measured not simply by how much the countries trade, but by how much they produce together and sell internationally.

Has sovereignty become an excuse for economic failure?

This raises a politically uncomfortable question: have successive Sri Lankan governments invoked sovereignty to defend national independence while neglecting the industrial reforms necessary to exercise it? Concerns about Indian influence are legitimate, but the country’s broader economic record reveals a contradiction between protecting domestic markets and developing competitive domestic industries.

The World Bank’s 2024 analysis identified Sri Lanka’s trade regime as exceptionally restrictive, with an average tariff, including para-tariffs, of 17.6% in 2022. It found that high and unpredictable import duties increased manufacturers’ input costs and discouraged export-oriented production. A policy framework defended partly through domestic protection was therefore making it harder for domestic businesses to compete internationally.

The controversy surrounding the proposed Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement illustrates the political dimension. During negotiations in 2016 and 2017, opposition parties and professional organisations raised concerns about competition, employment and national interests. Some objections warranted serious consideration, yet the debate frequently centred on whether economic opening endangered sovereignty rather than how Sri Lanka could develop industries capable of benefiting from expanded access. Negotiations resumed in 2023, but the underlying challenge of industrial competitiveness remains.

This is the paradox of defensive sovereignty: a State may seek independence by insulating its economy while simultaneously weakening the productive foundations on which meaningful independence depends. Sri Lanka’s industrial shortcomings cannot be attributed exclusively to anti-Indian politics; civil conflict, fiscal instability and governance failures are central explanations. Nevertheless, sovereignty cannot become a substitute for economic strategy, nor can protection be presumed beneficial merely because it is presented as patriotic.

Economic integration must strengthen national capability

Global production networks are being reorganised amid geopolitical competition, technological change and supply-chain diversification. Smaller economies struggle to compete independently against established industrial powers, but regional manufacturing networks offer opportunities for specialised production. Sri Lanka’s maritime location, workforce and existing industrial capabilities could support integration if accompanied by technological upgrading and consistent investment policy.

Indian investment already provides opportunities for cooperation, but investment volume alone cannot establish developmental success. Partnerships must be assessed through skilled employment, domestic procurement, technology transfer and export performance, supported by transparent contracts, predictable taxation and competition safeguards. Sri Lanka’s geographical advantages require similar discipline.
Colombo’s transshipment role and investments such as the Colombo West International Terminal create opportunities for logistics and maritime services, while Trincomalee’s potential in energy infrastructure warrants transparent commercial assessment. Without complementary industries, Sri Lanka risks becoming a location through which regional commerce passes rather than an economy that contributes meaningfully to its production.

Cultural proximity is an advantage, not an economic strategy

The civilisational relationship provides an unusually deep foundation for cooperation. Buddhism’s transmission from India, the incorporation of Hindu-associated deities into Buddhist practice and centuries of architectural and commercial exchange demonstrate interconnected societies capable of transforming external influences into local traditions. Contemporary relationships retain substantial people-to-people connections, including tourism, education and professional exchange.

Nevertheless, historical familiarity cannot guarantee equitable economic outcomes. Shared culture does not automatically generate competitive industries or responsible political leadership. Cultural diplomacy gives bilateral relations depth, but institutional capacity determines their economic value.

Sovereignty begins with productive strength

Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 exposed the vulnerability of a state possessing formal political independence but insufficient economic resilience. India’s emergency assistance of approximately $4 billion demonstrated the importance of cooperation, yet financial support cannot substitute for sustainable prosperity. The World Bank’s October 2026 assessment reported that Sri Lanka had returned to pre-crisis economic output levels, while poverty remained elevated at an estimated 16.9% in 2025. Stabilisation remains indispensable, but recovery without productive transformation risks preserving underlying vulnerabilities.

This suggests a broader principle of international relations: productive sovereignty. Building upon the established distinction between interdependence and asymmetric dependence, the concept holds that a smaller state’s strategic autonomy depends not exclusively on its capacity to resist external influence, but on its ability to generate economic capabilities that strengthen its bargaining position. Interdependence reinforces sovereignty when it produces technology, export markets and negotiating alternatives; it undermines sovereignty when it concentrates economic power without developing domestic productivity.

Sri Lanka must consequently maintain diversified international partnerships while developing industries that make cooperation mutually valuable. The objective is not freedom from economic relationships, but freedom from negotiating them through structural weakness. Integration with India should therefore be neither unconditional nor instinctively rejected; it must be judged by whether it expands Sri Lanka’s long-term economic and strategic choices.

An ancient relationship deserves a more ambitious future

Sri Lanka’s civilisational history demonstrates that engagement with India need not entail the erosion of national identity. Religious, intellectual and architectural influences crossed the Palk Strait and became part of a distinctly Sri Lankan civilisation. Modern economic diplomacy demands comparable confidence, strengthened by transparent negotiations and institutions capable of protecting national interests.

For decades, political debate has questioned whether closer relations with India threaten sovereignty. The more consequential question is whether successive governments have constructed an economy sufficiently productive to exercise sovereignty meaningfully. India’s ascent will reshape South Asia regardless of Sri Lanka’s participation, but the island retains the ability to determine whether its enterprises become valuable participants in that transformation or remain peripheral to it.

Sri Lanka’s greatest strategic vulnerability may not be that India is becoming too powerful, but that Sri Lanka has remained too economically unprepared to negotiate confidently with that power. More than two millennia of history have made the countries neighbours in civilisation, and geography has made them neighbours in commerce. Whether they become genuine partners in prosperity will depend not on sentimental friendship or political rhetoric, but on Sri Lanka’s willingness to transform proximity into productive strength.

(The author specialises in political accountability, governance, human rights, democracy, public policy and international affairs. She is also the Founder and Executive Director of Gamindi Foundation, a Sri Lankan non-governmental organisation)

title: Beneficial Ownership registration:  When compliance becomes a burden on businesses | Daily FT
summary:
