A few days ago, while sitting in a coffee shop, I heard an advertisement promoting its online ordering app. “Grab it and Go”, it went on “, Don’t wait in line. Join online and walk away with your order,” it proclaimed. I smiled at the clever message, but it made me think about our own experience with online systems introduced by regulatory institutions.

In many cases, going online doesn’t eliminate queues. We struggle through complicated digital procedures, only to end up visiting the relevant offices and standing in physical queues to complete the process.

It seems we have perfected a new form of digital administration: First, join the queue online, and then join it again in person.

This is a concern worth examining as Sri Lanka moves towards mandatory digital compliance, particularly with the introduction of Beneficial Ownership registration.

Beneficial Ownership (BO) registration, introduced by the Registrar of Companies (ROC), is an important step towards transparency and accountability in the corporate sector. Knowing who ultimately owns or controls a company supports good governance and helps prevent companies from being misused for illegal activities, such as conmen hiding behind corporate structures.

The other main aspect is identifying an individual as a beneficial owner who is not a shareholder legally recognised as a natural person. 

The problem is not the requirement itself, which professionals generally accept. The problem is how it is being implemented: a complicated reporting and approval process, delays, repeated visits to the Registrar’s office, technical difficulties, and penalties on companies that cannot complete their statutory work because of delays in the Government system. For many company secretaries, including lawyers, accountants and business owners, a measure meant to improve transparency has become a major administrative and financial burden.

A final warning, but where is the relief for businesses?

On 28 October, the Registrar issued a notice described as a final warning on BO compliance. It states that non-compliance could attract a fine of Rs. 1 million or imprisonment for up to 10 years.

Nobody argues that companies may ignore their legal responsibilities. But an authority that threatens such penalties must also provide a system through which those responsibilities can be fulfilled. Companies and their secretaries are still struggling with the online system, waiting for approvals and making repeated visits for help.

The system also assumes a level of digital skill that many directors may not have. A Government survey has reportedly found that only 38% of the population can use a computer independently, and many of them are schoolchildren and young adults. Directors from older generations and small businesses often need professional help, which adds cost.

The most unfair consequence is financial. Companies must file Annual Returns and other statutory documents within set periods, and late filing brings fines. Yet a company secretary cannot proceed with the Annual Return until the BO registration is approved. A company that uploads everything on time can still miss its deadline because the Registrar’s process is incomplete, and penalties begin to accumulate. 

Two practical solutions:

nRecognise the online submission date:. The date on which documents are successfully uploaded should count as the date of compliance, subject to later verification and correction. The postal service works this way: for registered post, the date stamp is treated as the date of receipt, because the sender is not responsible for delays in between.

nWaive or extend deadlines:  If the Registrar’s office cannot process applications in time, the Government should announce a temporary waiver or extension for companies that have submitted their documents online.

It is unreasonable to expect companies to pay penalties for delays beyond their control. Compliance must be a two-way responsibility.

A digital system with a manual bottleneck

Documents are uploaded online, but the process does not move automatically. A first-level officer must check and approve them, then pass them to a second level, and then a third, before any further action can be taken.

Officers are understood to have around 35,000 files to attend to. That may not be the number of pending files, but it shows the scale of the workload. If the system depends on a limited number of officers to examine every submission, delays are inevitable.

Professionals who have uploaded all the required documents still report visiting the Registrar’s office repeatedly to follow up, sometimes as many as five times. Regularly visiting government offices helps build rapport with officials, making them more sympathetic and willing to help move matters forward more quickly. Whether that is true or not, a statutory service should work through a clear, transparent process that treats every applicant the same.

A system not designed for its users

Moving Government services online should save time and money for everyone. With the BO website, professionals report the opposite, and several IT professionals who have examined it have questioned its design and user-friendliness.

A good digital system is built around its users’ needs, not the developers’ technical knowledge. For the BO website, that means:

A system that sends users back to the office to find out what is happening to documents already submitted online has missed one of the main purposes of digitalisation.

None of this means Sri Lanka should hold back on technology or AI, which can bring enormous benefits. But an online system does not understand the stress a company secretary feels when facing an official deadline. Technology should help people, not leave them feeling helpless.

When one company’s delay affects several others

Complicated ownership structures make matters worse. A company secretary recently explained one case using a diagram, which can be simplified as follows:

This creates multiple layers of corporate ownership, making it difficult to trace the chain back to the actual individuals who ultimately own or control the company.

Multiple layers of ownership are not illegal. BO registration exists to identify the natural persons who ultimately own or control these companies. The difficulty is that the secretary responsible for the company at the end of the chain cannot obtain BO approval because some companies higher up have not yet received their own. One company’s registration therefore depends on several others.

The company’s Annual Return is due, and the statutory deadline has passed, but it cannot be filed without BO approval. Is it reasonable to hold one company responsible for delays caused by other companies in its ownership structure, which may themselves be waiting for the Registrar?

This also raises a question: who analyses these, and how often? Should the law be amended to hold a company responsible for reporting this information as a needed to know basis?

One size does not fit all

The BO requirements appear to be applied in the same way to every registered company, regardless of activity, ownership structure or financial capacity. Special consideration may be justified for:

nGovernment-owned companies, which may need a different reporting procedure given their public ownership and existing accountability arrangements. What do they report, and where? The Treasury can have a list of all of its companies and so forth.

This does not mean automatic exemption from transparency requirements. But the Government should ask whether every category needs the same procedures and compliance costs. A risk-based approach, with simplified procedures or legally justified exemptions, would be more practical than a one-size-fits-all procedure.

A Company Secretary recently brought to my attention a case involving an international organisation seeking to establish its presence in Sri Lanka. The registration process has reportedly remained pending for nearly six months because the Registrar of Companies (ROC) requires the organisation to use a rubber stamp or corporate seal. This is despite the fact that many developed countries have moved away from the traditional requirement for corporate seals. The organisation has submitted an explanatory letter setting out its position, but this has not been accepted by the ROC.

This raises a broader question as to whether our registration procedures are keeping pace with evolving international corporate practices, or whether outdated administrative requirements are unnecessarily discouraging international organisations from establishing a presence in Sri Lanka. This is an example of bureaucratic obstacles to investment and ease of doing business.

For years, successive Governments have encouraged business owners to register as limited liability companies rather than operate as sole proprietorships or partnerships. Yet reports suggest some companies are now considering voluntary winding-up because of the added requirements, difficulties and costs, and some owners may revert to sole proprietorships or partnerships.

There is no benefit in encouraging businesses to become companies while making it harder for them to remain companies. Small and medium-sized businesses, in particular, may struggle with the cost of professional services, repeated visits to Government offices and the risk of penalties. The Government should examine the wider economic impact of the BO system, not treat it only as a compliance exercise.

Collecting information is not the same as using it

Banks in Sri Lanka already collect BO information when an account is opened, along with details of directors, authorised signatories and people who control the account. They are expected to carry out customer checks and monitor transactions for suspicious activity.

Has there been any publicly reported case where BO information alone helped identify money laundering, terrorist financing or drug-related activity? Such examples would show the practical value of collecting this information at scale. Of course, identifying a beneficial owner is not enough to establish wrongdoing. It must be examined alongside bank transactions, financial records, and other information.

The Registrar’s office already appears to be struggling to process the submissions it receives. Does it have enough officers with the necessary knowledge and technical skills to examine this information, identify suspicious ownership structures and pass findings to the investigating authorities? Collecting thousands of records is one thing; analysing them to uncover illegal activity is quite another.

The authorities should look beyond collection. The Registrar should study how neighbouring countries maintain, verify, and use their BO registers, and seek technical assistance from bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank to improve the system, train officers, and link the Registrar, banks, and the Financial Intelligence Unit.

The success of a BO register should be measured not by how many companies have submitted information, but by how effectively that information is used to improve transparency, prevent financial crime and protect the public interest.

What needs to be done

The Registrar of Companies and the Government should consider the following:

Speed and accountability

Fairness to companies

System and support

An Institutional Question

Another issue also deserves attention. The Registrar of Companies (ROC), which administers Beneficial Ownership registration, currently functions under the Ministry of Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Co-operative Development. While the Ministry has an important mandate covering trade, consumer protection, food security and co-operative development, Beneficial Ownership registration is fundamentally a corporate governance, transparency and financial integrity function.

The Ministry of Finance, meanwhile, has a broader responsibility for creating an economic environment that facilitates rapid development and investment. Perhaps it is time to reconsider whether the ROC should be elevated to a more prominent institutional position under the Ministry of Finance, with the authority, resources, and technical capacity needed to fulfil its expanding responsibilities.

Corporate transparency is not merely a regulatory requirement; it is a foundation for investor confidence and a modern economy. Shouldn’t the institution responsible for safeguarding it be positioned accordingly?

A final question for policymakers

BO registration is an important requirement, but good legislation and good administration must go together. A compliance system should help businesses meet their legal obligations, not prevent them from doing so.

If the Government wants businesses to operate transparently, it must ensure its own institutions do the same: efficiently and accountably. The question is not whether Sri Lanka should adopt modern technology, which it certainly should. The question is whether the technology is properly designed, adequately tested and supported by people who understand the needs of those who use it.

The Government should not penalise businesses for delays created by its own administrative machinery. Digitalisation should make doing business easier, not turn company administration into a burden that pushes businesses to abandon the corporate structure altogether.

title: Budget blues | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:22
-     - 45

President and Finance Minister 

Anura Kumara Dissanayake

Deputy Finance Minister 

Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando

The national Budget for 2027 which was announced by President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake in a stoic speech in parliament, was met with contrasting responses. The essence of a national Budget can be distilled by observing the reactions it provokes as much as by the numbers attached to Budget lines and the rhetoric in the Budget speech. 

Economists, business leaders, professional bodies, think tanks and rating agencies were quick to endorse the economic policies crafted by the National People’s Power (NPP). Their commentaries mainly raised concerns about the implementation of the policies and urged the Government to reform the public sector, which they saw as being the main obstacle to progress.

Apart from some reservations voiced about the dependence on a volatile market to deliver on investments and export-oriented growth, the ideological consensus between NPP’s Budget for 2027 and business leaders was apparent. The Opposition parties in parliament were disarmed by the convergence of policy interests across the aisles to effectively challenge its contents.

In contrast, the usual buzz around Budget announcements was largely absent among ordinary Sri Lankans. Households who were hopeful about receiving some relief on taxes of essential items, tariffs on basic utilities and household debt were disappointed.

Sri Lanka is now ranked one of the lowest in terms of minimum wage when adjusted for purchasing power. Year-on-year headline inflation has increased to above 8% pinching on household Budgets that had already suffered due to significant price adjustments and wage repression in the aftermath of the economic crisis, the burden of which is disproportionately borne by women. Addressing the cost-of-living pressures should have been an obvious policy priority in the 2027 Budget.

Stability and growth?

The positive report card given by the business community and economic experts is no assurance of sound policies or smooth sails ahead. Recall the responses to former President Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s infamous Budget with generous tax concessions to corporates, not even a tinge of the economic doom that was awaiting the country made it into their glowing post-Budget analyses. It only
means that their interests have been safeguarded by the NPP Government.

The Government, along with the business and economic experts, have repeatedly highlighted the 2027 Budget as hailing the transformation from, “economic stability to economic growth.” However, economic stability cannot be judged by fiscal discipline or macro data alone. The Budget does not convey a clear plan for how foreign debt and reserves will be managed in the future. Therefore, it is not possible to assess the soundness of the Government’s promise of macro-economic stability. 

Any mention of achieving economic stability rings hollow in the ears of the working people as their lives have been destabilised by harsh austerity policies continued by the NPP Government, climate disasters and volatility caused by the wars abroad. The recent release of preliminary data from HIES reveal a troubling picture of poverty and households mired in debt. 

Sri Lanka’s debt sustainability agreement negotiated by the previous Ranil Wickremesinghe Government and accepted by the NPP without renegotiations includes macro-linked bonds which is determined by economic growth rates. Higher economic growth in the consequent years will only increase the country’s debt burden rather than result in benefits for the people. Furthermore, economic growth alone will not result in redistribution without economic policies to facilitate it. Budget 2027 does not include a vision for redistribution.

One way in which a policy of redistribution could have been implemented is via the tax policies. However, the ratio of the public revenue composition remains unchanged between direct (24%) and indirect taxes (76%), extracting public revenues excessively from low-income earners while providing little in return to them. Apart from widening the scope of assets for Capital Gains Tax, no effort has been made to tax the super-rich who often hide their wealth in corporate holdings and differed dividends.

What is in it for the people?

In a preemptive special statement before the Budget announcement, the Deputy Minister of Finance Anil Jayantha Fernando reportedly urged the public to evaluate the Budget on its broader economic direction rather than on welfare benefits or tax concessions. 

The Budget is thin on welfare benefits, with a mere 0.6% of GDP allocation, sufficient to cover only a fraction of the most vulnerable sections of our society – low-income families, disabled, those with chronic illness and the elderly, while leaving many households out. 

Budget 2027 provides no clear vision for how the NPP Government hopes to address poverty or growing inequalities. Although the poverty level has increased to what it was 10 years ago, the Budgetary amounts for low-income families have remained unchanged. 

The Budget fails to adequately provision for extremities caused by the El Nino effect on the country’s fragile food system, livelihoods, health and education, even though the main factor contributing to why half the population are multidimensionally vulnerable is the inability to withstand climate events (UNDP).

Education and health sectors are given priority in the expenditure heads, however, the low GDP allocations of 1.91% and 1.87% respectively, relegates Sri Lanka to one of the lowest spending countries for these sectors.

The Deputy Finance Minister’s assurance that the Budget ensures public funds benefit the citizens, through “quality investments, increasing export-oriented production and employment generation,” holds little truth.
Only a dismal amount - 0.7% of GDP - is invested in the agriculture sector, where most Sri Lankans depend on for their livelihoods. 

Apart from continuing housing projects and Rs. 200 allowance which is riddled with implementation challenges, no substantial provisions to address the neglect and exploitation of the plantation workers are included in the Budget.

The percentage (43%) of unemployment among educated youth which is the highest in the region is alarming (IMF Asia Pacific Outlook April 2026). Yet the Budget does not propose a clear plan for job creation, including to absorb the job losses from a flailing IT industry. Meanwhile, in a questionable proposal, 18-year-olds are being lured into investing in risky capital markets by providing share portfolios.

In terms of tax concessions, the relief provided to income (Rs. 16 billion) and import taxes (Rs. 10 billion) is large compared to the relief on Value Added Tax of only Rs. 2.9 billion. A significant portion of the public and private sector workers’ monthly salaries fall below Rs. 100 000. Although gradual Budgetary increases on salaries were granted over three years, discrepancies exist in public sector salary scales.

The longstanding salary issues of the biggest group of the public sector cadre, of 225 000 professionals in teachers’ service, remains unresolved. Teacher unions have now called for a token strike if the Government
does not agree to grant the remaining two-thirds of the salary adjustments promised according to the Subodini Report and in the interim a cost-of-living allowance of Rs. 25 000.

The working people of the country who voted in large numbers to bring the NPP to power have been patient for the last two years to find its footing in its first stint in Government. The third consecutive Budget under NPP’s leadership was a massive let down for those who held out hope for some share of the economic gains to be redistributed to them. Their patience is now beginning to falter when Budgetary concessions and investments fail to reach a large section of the voting public. 

Indeed, a Budget that is crafted to win over the IMF, which is due for a visit to the country next week, is unlikely to be popular among the voters. It has demonstrated that a Government shackled by the conditionalities of the IMF cannot truly deliver economic justice. The NPP Government should not shackle the whole country to another IMF agreement.

(The author is a PhD Candidate in Education at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a member of the Feminist Collective for Economic Justice)

title: Five reasons Sri Lanka should go for another IMF program | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:21
-     - 85

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake chairs a meeting with an IMF delegation during its visit to Colombo in July 2026

Sri Lanka’s economic recovery in terms of macroeconomic indicators has been a remarkable story of success and resilience. From a nation posting negative growth of around 7%, inflation at nearly 70% and market interest rates at over 30%, Sri Lanka has largely stabilised thanks to its fiscal policies and the IMF. But currently Sri Lanka is facing external shocks such as the Mideast war, Russia-Ukraine war, rising global interest rates, El Nino and trade pattern changes globally. The most devastating impact has been the Mideast war, which is leading to a high fuel import bill, severely hampering Sri Lanka’s ability to build gross reserves.

But as Sri Lanka’s reserves are not meeting projections, global interest rates are high, the IMF program is coming to an end and debt repayment levels are increasing from 2028, a critical question is, “Should Sri Lanka go for another IMF program”? Let me give the case for it.

Low gross reserves

Sri Lanka has lagged behind in terms of getting to the IMF’s projected (not target) figures in terms of gross official reserves. Currently as of October 2026, we are at $7.1 billion in reserves. Fitch projects gross reserves to be at $7.7 billion by the end of this year. The IMF report of May 2026 projected gross reserves to be at $8.6 billion by the end of this year. Sri Lanka is still going to fall back by almost $1 billion from the reserves projected by the IMF just 6 months ago, if we get to $7.7 billion by the end of this year (as Fitch projects). But when looking at the March 2023 IMF report which the program was signed with, that report projected that Sri Lanka would have reserves of $10.9 billion by the end of 2026. We will be short of the end-of-2026 projection made by the IMF in March 2023, by close to $3.2 billion, even if we are to have reserves of $7.7 billion by the end of this year. March 2023 IMF projections were not targets and were always subject to change, but I am raising the point to show how far we have fallen back. An IMF program will be a strong safeguard for Sri Lanka, when gross reserves are not doing as well as projected.

IMF brings confidence

Many people in Sri Lanka dismiss the IMF as saying it’s just $3 billion and if we can get an investment of such a figure, we would not need the IMF. I have explained this many times before, the IMF is much more than the $3 billion. The IMF is like a verification for the Sri Lankan economy. It is like an auditor where investors, international bond markets, bilaterals and other multilaterals trust the IMF to move forward with a country in most cases. At this juncture especially when Sri Lanka is facing turbulence due to external shocks, having the IMF on board is much better.

IMF is cheaper to borrow from than ISBs

As US 10 year Treasury yields hit 5.35% in October this year, borrowing costs are currently high due to high debt levels in developed countries, increasing inflation and financing being diverted to AI related spending. This will also mean that IMF borrowing costs also get higher but borrowing from the IMF is cheaper than issuing international sovereign bonds. Rather than issue a sovereign bond next year, 2027 (as projected by the IMF), Sri Lanka could borrow from the IMF. The other benefit is that borrowing from the IMF comes with technical assistance and IMF reviews of the economy at least twice a year.

Sovereign rating not enough

The current rating of B- by Fitch may not be enough to access international capital markets in 2027 at decent borrowing costs. The IMF has projected Sri Lanka issuing a Eurobond of $1.5 billion in 2027 but a further rating upgrade would give us better access to international capital markets. Another rating upgrade is not guaranteed in 2027 so it is best for Sri Lanka to grab what is within reach in March 2027 to safeguard itself from potential shocks. As gross reserves are not where they were projected to be even by the IMF in May 2026, Sri Lanka has little time.

Borrow from the IMF to pay the IMF back

Table 1 shows how much we have to pay back the IMF each year from 2026-2030.

As seen in Table 1, Sri Lanka will be paying $2.194 billion back to the IMF from 2026 to 2030. There is a saying which goes as “Borrowing from Peter to pay Paul”. I am saying, “Let us borrow from Peter to pay back Peter”. In the next 4 years (2027-2030), Sri Lanka is expected to pay back the IMF a sum of $1.848 billion. Another program can help neutralise this to some extent. This is not something new. Sri Lanka keeps borrowing from the World Bank and at the same time, Sri Lanka is paying back the World Bank for past loans. We can do a similar process with the IMF.

(The author is a Sri Lankan Economist. The views expressed in this article are strictly the author’s own personal opinions)

title: Budget 2027: Sri Lanka is running out of time. Trade agreements alone won’t save the economy | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:20
-     - 23

Budget 2027 has announced a committee to drive trade agreements across multiple countries

WHILE Sri Lanka debates trade agreements, the rest of Asia is building the future. India is racing towards a $ 5 trillion economy. Vietnam exports more than $ 370 billion annually. Bangladesh's apparel exports now exceed $ 50 billion. ASEAN is becoming the centre of global manufacturing growth. Regional supply chains are being redrawn, investment is shifting across Asia, and countries are competing aggressively for technology, talent and export market share. 

Sri Lanka, meanwhile, continues to debate whether it should embrace economic openness at all. That debate belongs to another era. As the country debates Budget 2027, the real question is not whether Sri Lanka needs more Free Trade Agreements (FTAs). It is whether Sri Lanka can become competitive enough to benefit from them before the opportunity passes. The greatest threat to the economy is no longer protectionism, inflation or even debt. It is irrelevant.

The recovery story masks a bigger problem

The Government points to encouraging economic indicators. Inflation has stabilised. Tourism has rebounded but stalled due to the Middle Eastern crisis. Remittances have improved significantly. Export earnings reached a record $ 17.25 billion in 2025, growing by 5.6%. Sri Lanka is poised to reach $ 20 billion this year. Which are positive signs.

But they are not signs of transformation. Sri Lanka's export earnings are still less than one-twentieth of Vietnam's exports. Apparel still accounts for nearly $ 5 billion of export income. Research and development spending remains below 0.2% of GDP, among the lowest in Asia. Exports remain heavily concentrated in a handful of products and markets. The uncomfortable truth is that Sri Lanka has recovered from a crisis without yet solving the weaknesses that caused it. A country of 22 million people cannot become prosperous by selling largely the same products to largely the same markets for another decade.

The FTA debate has been a distraction

For years, Sri Lanka's economic debate has centred on whether FTAs are good or bad. The evidence from Asia suggests this is the wrong question. Vietnam did not become an export powerhouse because it signed trade agreements. It became successful because it simultaneously invested in industrial zones, logistics infrastructure, technical education, foreign investment attraction and export competitiveness.

 Bangladesh did not become the world's second-largest apparel exporter because of preferential market access. It built factories, skills and scale. South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore did not become advanced economies because of trade liberalisation alone. They invested relentlessly in productivity, technology, innovation and human capital. Trade agreements created opportunities. Competitiveness converted opportunities into growth. Sri Lanka continues to confuse the two.

India's rise should concern every policymaker

Nowhere is Sri Lanka's challenge more evident than in its relationship with India. Bilateral trade exceeded $ 5.3 billion in 2025, however, Sri Lankan exports to India is just $ 1 billion. When I was Chairman of the Sri Lanka Export Development Board around 20 years back, it was at 0.5 billion dollars. Which is the slow pace of export growth. Whilst some celebrate these numbers, they should also raise different questions. A country situated less than 30 kilometres from one of the world's fastest-growing major economies globally exports only $ 1 billion worth of goods to a market of 1.4 billion people for a tiny share of 0.12%. Why? The answer cannot simply be market access. India exports machinery, pharmaceuticals, vehicles, petroleum products and industrial inputs because it possesses scale, productivity and industrial depth.

 Sri Lanka exports far less because it has not developed comparable industrial capabilities. The gap is not geographic. The gap is competitive. And it is widening. While India is investing billions of dollars through Make in India, Production Linked Incentive programs, logistics corridors, semiconductor manufacturing and digital infrastructure, Sri Lanka is still arguing about whether trade agreements themselves are beneficial. The rest of Asia settled that debate years ago.

The trade deficit is not the problem

Critics frequently point to Sri Lanka's trade deficit with India as evidence that the Indo-Lanka FTA has failed. That interpretation is politically convenient but economically misleading. Nearly 90% of imports from major trading partners such as India and China occur outside FTA concessions, with importers paying full duties and choosing those products anyway because they remain competitive on price, quality and reliability. That single statistic reveals an uncomfortable reality. 

Competitiveness is driving trade, not tariff concessions. Likewise, Sri Lanka's export challenges are not primarily caused by a lack of agreements. They are caused by: Low productivity, High production costs, Weak innovation, Limited economies of scale, Skills shortages, Inadequate industrial sophistication In other words, Sri Lanka has a competitiveness problem disguised as a trade policy problem.

The US tariff shock is a warning

Recent developments in the United States should be a wake-up call. According to IPS estimates, Sri Lanka could have faced effective tariff rates of almost 30%, with apparel tariffs exceeding 36% and potential export losses of more than $ 600 million. Nearly 16,000 jobs could have been affected. Subsequently, the effective rate was reduced by Trump, but the most important lesson is not the tariff itself. It is the exposure. 

Any economy whose export performance can be significantly disrupted by a policy decision in a single market has failed to diversify sufficiently. Sri Lanka's dependence on a limited number of products and destinations is becoming a strategic economic risk. Diversification is no longer desirable. It is urgent.

Asia is moving faster than Sri Lanka

The world economy is increasingly centred in Asia. The RCEP bloc accounts for roughly 30% of global GDP and trade. East Asia's middle class expanded from approximately 834 million consumers in 2016 to more than 1.1 billion by 2022. By 2030, one in every three middle-class consumers globally is expected to live in East Asia. This is where future demand will come from. This is where future investment will flow. This is where future supply chains will be built, just like what we saw in the recent Nvidia debacle. The critical question is whether Sri Lanka will be part of that growth story. Or whether it will watch from the sidelines.

What Budget 2027 must deliver

Budget 2027 should not be measured by the number of committees established or agreements negotiated. It should be judged against six questions: Will it increase productivity? Will it raise investment in innovation and research beyond the current 0.2% of GDP? Will it create new export sectors in electronics, medical technology, AI, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing? Will it modernise customs, logistics and trade facilitation? Will it address severe skills shortages across industry? Will it help Sri Lankan firms become globally competitive? If the answer is no, additional FTAs will simply become additions to an already long list of underutilised agreements.

The real choice facing Sri Lanka

The debate is no longer between protectionism and liberalisation. That is yesterday's argument. The real choice facing Sri Lanka is between competitiveness and irrelevance. Trade agreements can open doors. They cannot create productive factories. They cannot build innovative companies. They cannot develop skilled workers. They cannot substitute for economic reform. Only competitiveness can do that. And that is why Budget 2027 matters.

 The window for reform is still open. But it is narrowing quickly as India, Vietnam, Indonesia and other Asian economies accelerate ahead. Sri Lanka's challenge is no longer whether it should join the race. The challenge is that the race has already started. The longer the country delays, the harder it will become to catch up. Budget 2027 must therefore be more than a fiscal statement. It must be a competitive Budget. Otherwise, Sri Lanka risks becoming a spectator in Asia's economic rise rather than a participant in it.

 (The author is the only Sri Lankan to have been the Chairman of the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, and Sri Lanka Tourism and to be appointed as the Commissioner General of World Expo - Milan, Italy. Currently, he serves as the World Rural Tourism Council (WRTC) Vice Chairman. He is an alumnus of Harvard University).

title: Unpaid care work: Sri Lanka’s invisible economy demands policy action | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 27 November 2026 00:02
-     - 0

By Shanika Sriyananda

Mothers of children with disabilities often endure immense emotional and psychological distress, including stress, depression and anxiety, while facing isolation and marginalisation within their own families and society. Their contribution to their families through household chores and the demanding responsibility of caring for their children with disabilities often goes unnoticed, much like the unpaid work undertaken by millions of other women.

From preparing meals and cleaning homes to caring for children, older persons and family members with disabilities, millions of hours of work sustain Sri Lankan households every day.

Yet much of this labour remains invisible in economic calculations, unrecognised in public policy and disproportionately shouldered by women and girls.

“A mother who comes to our daycare centre for children said she sleeps for a while as her youngest child is safely looked after in the centre. This shows how women sacrifice their time for the betterment of the family by working from dawn to dusk. But her contribution to caregiving responsibilities was not paid or appreciated,” Aneesa Firthous of the Islamic Women’s Association for Research and Empowerment (IWARE), based in Batticaloa, said.

Speaking at a panel discussion on community-led care, she highlighted the need to change attitudes towards women's caregiving responsibilities to enable women and girls to improve their living standards and personal wellbeing.

“It is very difficult to bring about attitude changes in the Muslim community, as it is still a patriarchal society. There are still girls who get married at a young age and, throughout their lives, shoulder all the household unpaid work, as society still believes that looking after children and elders and doing household work belong to women,” she said, stressing the need to make women aware of the importance of sharing responsibilities at home.

Drawing on the findings of their research, community-led women's leaders from Batticaloa, Kandy, Anuradhapura and Jaffna said many young boys and older men still believe that mothers and wives who remain at home are not doing any work.

“They think women are just at home and are not doing any work. We gave them a timetable to make them understand the amount of work those women at home do daily. We also have street dramas and short films to make males and young boys understand the importance of sharing responsibilities at home,” they said.

Women and girls shoulder a disproportionate share of household and caregiving responsibilities, limiting their economic opportunities and wellbeing. As Sri Lanka moves towards a dedicated National Policy on Unpaid Care Work, translating commitments into practical, adequately funded solutions is becoming an urgent priority.

The unequal distribution of unpaid care work continues to place a disproportionate burden on women and girls in Sri Lanka, restricting their access to employment, education, economic independence and personal wellbeing, and prompting renewed calls for a dedicated national policy backed by effective implementation.

According to the Sri Lanka Child Youth Survey 2017, conducted by the Department of Census and Statistics, 87.3% of women and girls aged 10 years and above participated in unpaid domestic and caregiving activities, compared with 59.7% of men and boys.

The figures highlight a persistent gender divide in household responsibilities, reflecting social norms that continue to regard caring for children, older persons, persons with disabilities and other family members as primarily women's work.

The economic consequences are significant. According to the Labour Force Survey 2021, women accounted for 73% of Sri Lanka's economically inactive population, with 59% of these women identifying care responsibilities as the primary reason for remaining outside the labour force.

With women's labour force participation remaining low, women's organisations and development partners are calling for a comprehensive national policy that recognises care as an essential economic and social contribution while establishing mechanisms to reduce and redistribute these responsibilities.

The call was made at the third National Convening on Recognising Unpaid Care Work, organised by The Asia Foundation and Women and Media Collective (WMC), with the support of Global Affairs Canada, in Colombo recently.

Held annually since 2024 to mark the International Day of Care and Support, the convening this year was themed ‘From Policy to Community-driven Solutions: Engaging Communities to Share Unpaid Care Responsibilities’.

The Canadian-funded project, Unpaid Care Work in Sri Lanka, supports national and local efforts to recognise, redistribute and reduce the disproportionate load of unpaid care work carried by women and girls, while representing and responding to their rights and needs.

Bringing together government representatives, development partners, civil society organisations, women's groups and private sector stakeholders, the event highlighted progress towards a draft National Policy on Unpaid Care Work and community-led initiatives addressing care needs across the country.

However, participants stressed that the challenge now lies in ensuring that policy commitments translate into tangible improvements in the lives of women and girls.

Economic implications

Canadian High Commissioner to Sri Lanka and the Maldives Isabelle Martin highlighted the economic implications of the unequal distribution of unpaid care work, noting that women continue to undertake a disproportionate share of responsibilities for caring for children, older persons and households.

“Across Sri Lanka, women continue to carry a disproportionate share of unpaid care responsibilities, caring for children, elderly persons and households. Yet, this work remains largely unrecognised and undervalued,” she said, adding that the consequences were significant: unpaid care responsibilities limit women's access to employment, reduce economic opportunities and contribute to persistent gender inequalities.

Martin highlighted that nearly 60% of unemployed women in Sri Lanka identify care responsibilities as the main reason they remain outside the labour force.

“Research shows that recognising and valuing unpaid care work could make a substantial contribution to Sri Lanka’s economic growth and social wellbeing. Reducing the unequal burden of care will enable more women to participate in the labour force and contribute to the inclusive economy,” she said.

Martin said the initiative was guided by the five Rs framework – Recognise, Reduce, Redistribute, Represent and Respond – and worked at both policy and community levels.

Commending the progress made towards the National Policy and Action Plan for Unpaid Care Work, she said it was an important step towards ensuring that care work was recognised not only as a private responsibility but also as a public policy responsibility and priority.

“It is equally important that the project strengthens the voices and leadership of women's rights organisations and women advocates who are driving change in their communities,” the High Commissioner said, adding that Canada remains firmly committed to supporting women's empowerment, gender equality and inclusive governance in Sri Lanka.

Call for coordinated policy implementation

Women and Child Affairs Minister Saroja Savithri Paulraj said women's labour force participation currently stands at only 32%, highlighting the need to address the unequal distribution of unpaid care responsibilities.

Citing the 2017 survey findings, she emphasised that 87.3% of women and girls aged 10 and above participated in unpaid domestic and caregiving activities, compared with 59.7% of men and boys.

“These figures highlight the unequal distribution of care responsibilities and the need for meaningful action,” the Minister said.

She noted that Sri Lanka had already introduced several policies and initiatives relevant to care and social protection, including the National Policy on Gender Equality and Women Empowerment, the Women Empowerment Act 2024, the National Policy on Child Day Care Facilities in Sri Lanka 2024, the National Social Protection Policy 2024, the National Action Plan on Social Care and the National Policy for Elders.

While these frameworks provide important foundations, Paulraj stressed that they must be complemented by a dedicated policy addressing the structural causes of the unequal distribution of unpaid care work.

“While these frameworks strengthen services and support for people who need care, we must also address the everyday realities of women who spend countless hours caring for children, older persons, persons with disabilities and other family members, often without any provision of support,” she said.

Paulraj noted that unpaid care work was connected to several areas of public policy, including labour rights, social protection, early childhood development, health, disability inclusion and support for older persons.

“Instead, care must be recognised and shared systematically among families, communities, the state and the private sector,” she said.

The Minister added that policy implementation would require coordinated action across government institutions, development partners, women's organisations, service providers, trade unions, researchers and the private sector.

Paulraj acknowledged the contribution of grassroots women's organisations in raising awareness, conducting community discussions, undertaking research and advocating for change.

“Through awareness-raising, community discussions, research and advocacy, they are bringing unpaid care work into public discussion and helping ensure that women's experiences and voices are reflected in the policy process,” she said.

However, the Minister cautioned that women's organisations could not be expected to fill gaps in public services indefinitely.

“Often with limited funding and by relying on women's unpaid labour, these organisations need appropriate recognition, resources and support to sustain their work,” she said.

Paulraj emphasised that the ultimate objective was to ensure that women had greater opportunities to participate in education, employment and public life while having time for rest and their own aspirations.

“Policy is only as meaningful as the difference it makes in people's lives,” she said, emphasising the need to have a society where care is valued, shared and supported, and where no woman or girl is held back from realising her full potential because of unequal care responsibilities.

Need for structural reform

WMC Director - Programs for Gender and Political Economy Dr. Sepali Kottegoda said the organisation's work on unpaid care had evolved through more than a decade of research, advocacy and engagement with communities.

“The research and advocacy that WMC has been carrying out for more than a decade have been exciting and challenging,” she said. “With the Asia Foundation’s support, awareness-raising on social norms change and shared responsibility for unpaid care work at the community level by women's organisations is a significant marker in this journey.”

Kottegoda stressed that unpaid care work should be addressed as a structural issue affecting gender equality, labour force participation, poverty and human development, rather than being treated solely as a welfare concern.

“Challenges still remain. The category of labour remains confined to activities that are deemed to directly produce income, which contributes to the country’s GDP. But we need to strengthen awareness and policy acceptance that unpaid care work does contribute economic value within the household as well as to the larger economy,” she emphasised.

According to Dr. Kottegoda, unpaid care work reflects a broader reality: women's labour is both essential and invisible, while women are expected to perform those tasks without recognition or compensation.

“This reinforces the structural devaluation of care work in economic and policy frameworks,” she said.

Dr. Kottegoda, stressing the need to integrate unpaid care work into government budgeting, planning and monitoring, and to ensure that recognition is accompanied by concrete institutional action, said that the draft policy seeks to recognise care work as an essential contribution to families, communities and the national economy.

The draft National Policy on Unpaid Care Work, developed by WMC in collaboration with the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs, with support from The Asia Foundation and Global Affairs Canada, is currently under review and is expected to be submitted for Cabinet approval in 2026.

“Women's labour is both essential and invisible, but the expectation is that women will perform these tasks, regardless of recognition or compensation, reinforces the structural devaluation of care work in economic and policy frameworks,” she noted.

Dr. Kottegoda said that the draft labour reforms were considering extending paternity leave from three days to five days. “Still, we need to ask: how would this manifest in terms of sharing childcare or household chores?” she questioned.

The policy is aligned with Sri Lanka's constitutional principles and international commitments, including the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, and Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality.

Call for shared responsibility

The Asia Foundation's Country Representative for Sri Lanka and the Maldives, Johann Rebert, said the initiative had been driven by a commitment to place the experiences, needs and rights of women and girls at the centre of efforts to address unpaid care work.

“When we started this journey, we shared one important priority,” he said, adding that the priority was to challenge the perception that caring for families and communities was primarily women's work.

He said that care was a shared responsibility, with men and other family members, communities, the state and the private sector all having a role to play.

Rebert said the initiative had sought to generate evidence on how women from different communities experienced care responsibilities and to support solutions that responded to their realities.

Community-led solutions

While national policy development continues, women's organisations across Sri Lanka are already working to address unpaid care responsibilities through community-led initiatives.

The convening highlighted women-led, community-based daycare models for older persons, children and persons with disabilities in Jaffna, Batticaloa and Anuradhapura.

Community-led initiatives in Kurunegala, Nuwara Eliya, Hambantota and Batticaloa are also raising awareness about unpaid care work and advocating for a more equitable distribution of responsibilities.

These initiatives demonstrate how local organisations can respond to care needs while challenging the social norms that place the responsibility primarily on women.

At the panel discussions, women community leaders highlighted that access to affordable and accessible care services remains a major challenge. They explained that, for women who cannot afford private daycare or eldercare services, caring for family members can become a full-time responsibility, limiting their ability to seek employment or pursue other opportunities.

However, the growing demand for eldercare is adding to the pressure, as Sri Lanka is among the fastest-ageing countries in South Asia, and the increasing number of older persons is expected to intensify the demand for care services.

Women who frequently provide care for both children and older family members face growing demands on their time and energy.

The panellists highlighted that this situation had affected women's rights to education, paid employment, professional development and rest, as well as their physical and mental wellbeing. It affects women across all social and economic backgrounds.

It was also said that care was connected to several areas of public policy, including labour rights, social protection, early childhood development, health, disability inclusion and support for older persons.

At the discussions, the community-led women's organisations in Jaffna, Batticaloa and Anuradhapura emphasised the importance of developing women-led, community-based daycare models for older persons, children and persons with disabilities. They also highlighted community-led solutions in Kurunegala, Nuwara Eliya, Hambantota and Batticaloa that raise awareness and promote the need to share unpaid care work responsibilities among men and boys.

“Over 80% of men and boys in the estate sector still say that women are just staying at home. The work that women do from 4 am to 11 pm is not being recognised and valued. This change in thinking should start from the pre-school, giving importance to the sharing of care responsibilities,” the participants said.

Dr. Sanjana Hattotuwa

Dr.Sanjana Hattotuwa, who researches social media, artificial intelligence and their implications for human rights, political communication and democratic integrity, in this interview highlights concerns on civil liberties, digitisation and Artificial Intelligence (AI) arising from several new legislations introduced by the Government. Here are excerpts;

By Shakuntala Perera

Q: You are concerned of a ‘gap’ that exists with what you refer to as the manner in which each of the proposed laws comes under a ‘reasonable-sounding’ name such as online safety, anti-corruption and efficient public services, leaving room for opposition to them on their own terms. How serious a concern is this to the civil liberties thus exercised in the country?

A: It’s among the most serious concerns I have, because the name of a law settles public opinion about it long before anyone has read, let alone tested in court, what its clauses actually permit. Online safety, anti-corruption, the recovery of stolen assets, data protection, cybersecurity, counter-terrorism, organised crime and efficient public services are each very hard to argue against, and in a country that went bankrupt in 2022, whose public money was looted for decades and which lived through the Easter Sunday attacks in 2019, they are meant to be. Each instrument then invites its own consultation and its own critique, one at a time, so that lawyers take on the Online Safety Act, NGOs the NGO Bill, a handful of us the cybersecurity draft, and economists cheer digitalisation, and while every one of these responses is accurate, each deals with a single law in isolation.


The gap lies between what a law says it is for and what its text permits, and it widens sharply when the laws are read together, which is what I’ve called interaction design. Silencing an organisation in Sri Lanka won’t need a single, perfect authoritarian law. It needs a map of who you are, which the draft NGO law and a national digital identity supply, a means to contest what you say in public, which the Online Safety Act supplies, a route into your money, messages and devices, which the Anti-Corruption Act, the Proceeds of Crime Act and the PSTA and Prevention of Organised Crimes (POC) Bills supply, and systems that let one agency pass what it learns to another. Each piece has a defensible purpose, and that is what makes the architecture they form together so hard to see.

Opposing them on their own terms is hard precisely because those terms were chosen well, since nobody wants to be seen defending corruption, terrorism or organised crime, and so the critic is cast as an apologist for all three while the conversation never reaches the clause that lets a Deputy Inspector General obtain your call records and phone tower locations without a court order, or the one that makes failing to inform on a friend punishable by up to seven years in prison. Parliament’s own record bears this out, since in a study of 173 Hansards from January 2025 to September 2026 I found MPs arguing over cost, procurement and implementation, while human rights impact assessment, remedy and safeguards against surveillance barely featured at all. If those elected to scrutinise these laws debate the labels, it’s hardly surprising that citizens do too.

Q: In effect the laws that have been under the NPP Government’s express agenda threaten various aspects of basic rights such as speech, funding and also a right to organise?

A: Dissent in Sri Lanka today remains lawful, though each new statute makes it more costly to exercise. In August I counted at least 7 laws and draft laws since 2023 that bear directly on what citizens and organisations may say, publish, fund and organise, and the POC Bill, gazetted on 2 October, is the eighth.

On speech, the Online Safety Act’s section 12 still makes a “false statement” that threatens national security, public health or public order punishable by up to 5 years in prison, with a Commission the President appoints deciding what is false before any court does. The Act remains unrepealed and unamended despite repeated promises, its first prosecution concluded in April 2026, and it isn’t the state’s alone, since in April 2025 a private Bank obtained orders under it against websites and named Facebook, LinkedIn and X accounts discussing the bank’s own data breach. 

The revised PSTA adds up to 15 years for gathering or sharing information about police or military activity, with no test of whether that information was secret or whether sharing it did any harm, so a video of an arrest or a message telling friends where a police cordon is could each qualify, and the POC Bill adds up to 10 years for telling anyone that the police are investigating a group.

On funding, the quieter architecture of delay, disclosure and dependency already does more damage than any spyware. A survey of one hundred organisations recorded 69% facing difficulties accessing foreign funding, 50% struggling to open bank accounts, 57% reporting frequent banking problems and 21% postponing activities outright, and that is before the Anti-Corruption and Proceeds of Crime Acts, which allow accounts to be frozen and banking, phone and device records obtained on ex parte orders, are turned on a politically visible organisation.


On organising, the draft NGO law would catch any group of five or more people formed for non-profit purposes, make non-registration itself an offence, allow suspension without a judicial order on undefined grounds of sovereignty and national security, and have registration lapse every three years, while the POC Bill treats three people acting together as a possible criminal group and lets an undefined “suspicious association” count towards membership. 

The chilling effect of all this begins well before anyone is charged, and that is why it matters so much now, while the architecture is still being built.

Q: You are also concerned about the Government’s creation of a national digital identity system with a central population register and a national AI strategy. What given the country’s chequered political history raises serious concerns in you?

A: I want easier, better public services as much as anyone, and the country desperately needs functioning digital systems after the 2022 collapse. My concern begins with July 1983, when mobs moved through Colombo with voter registration lists, identifying Tamil homes, shops and factories street by street with help from the administration, the army and the police, and around 3,000 people were killed that week. 

Beyond the horror, I keep returning to the instrument, a paper register compiled for an unrelated purpose, held by the state and turned to targeting within days. Paper imposed friction, since a pogrom needed people to cross-reference lists by hand. A central digital identity resolves the same query in milliseconds, from anywhere, for every home at once, and it can run again and again. The mobs of 1983 needed no computer to act on their intent, though a digital register would have removed the friction that limited how far that intent could reach.

Consider what is being built. The Sri Lanka Unique Digital Identity, funded by a grant and built on face, fingerprint and iris biometrics, is due to issue its first identities by the end of this year, alongside a national data exchange whose “Ask Once” principle means what you give one agency becomes available to others. The Department for Registration of Persons describes its central population register as one that supports national security and exchanges information with other organisations, which is its own language and not mine. 

GovTech’s chief executive has spoken of biometric registration at birth and a country that is paperless, cashless and presence-less, which to me reads like a blueprint for what I’ve called surveillance by default, if not by design. Over Rs. 30 billion in the 2026 Budget went to biometric identification, revenue tracking, immigration, police data systems and financial transaction monitoring without any scrutiny of who controls the data.

All of this is being built ahead of the safeguards meant to govern it, since the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) commences only in part on 1 January 2027, and the order bringing it into force leaves out the rights to see, correct or erase your own data. The Lanka Government Cloud collapsed for nine days in 2025 with no accountability, a 2023 ransomware attack erased email for around 5,000 Government addresses, and in October I found at least 80 of around 640 live gov.lk websites running vulnerable versions of PHP. 

Not a single document, page or slide explaining the program exists in Sinhala or Tamil, which makes Sri Lanka, to my knowledge, the only country digitising this comprehensively without addressing most of its own citizens in their own languages. I’ve called it skyscrapers on a quagmire.

Given our history, negligence of this kind is dangerous, since the PTA, enacted in 1979 as a temporary measure, was used for decades against Tamils, Muslims, journalists and dissenters. Pandemic contact tracing saw military intelligence reach into the phone records of patients, social media was blocked in 2018 and 2019, and in August 2025 the Counter Terrorism Investigation Department summoned the president of the Mullaitivu Press Club over posts documenting excavation at the Chemmani mass grave. Our institutions have never distributed suspicion equally, and it’s silly to believe that digital systems designed and run by the same institutions will magically defend rights.

Q: It is fact that no one has seen the Cyber Security Bill the 3rd draft of which is with the AGs department. Why do you think the Government is functioning with such secrecy?

A: The secrecy around the Cybersecurity Bill fits a pattern. The Deputy Minister of Digital Economy told Parliament that a third draft went to the Attorney General in October and should become law in early 2027, yet the last public version dates from July 2023, and no one outside Government (and, I suspect, few within it) has read what replaced it. 

I can think of a few likely explanations, beginning with a drafting culture housed in the Ministries of Defence and Public Security that has never seen the public as a stakeholder, carried over intact from previous administrations. There’s also loss driving the text, since the Treasury lost $ 2.5 million to an email compromise between December 2025 and January 2026, through a system CERT had advised updating in 2023, and a Government legislating in the shadow of a loss like that can easily stop distinguishing between securing the state and surveilling its citizens.

Secrecy also carries a procedural cost, since, as with the Online Safety Act, citizens may first read the Bill only once it is gazetted, with a very short window to challenge it in the Supreme Court, and nothing at all once it is law. Sri Lanka needs a cybersecurity law, and an authority able to make institutions fix what they are told to fix. However, a Bill nobody outside Government has read can’t claim public consent, and a Government elected on the promise of system change should find that argument easy to accept.

Q: Can you draw comparisons of other global scenarios where such a wide-reaching surveillance mechanism through such a series of laws passed without any consultation from the rest of society has led to the concerns that you speak of coming true?

A: I would start closer to home, and with the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), which was passed in 1979 as a temporary law, with little debate, to deal with a specific threat. It stayed on the books for over four decades, was used against Tamils, Muslims, journalists and dissenters far beyond anything its sponsors claimed, and has drawn repeated UN calls for repeal ever since. Section 3 of the ICCPR Act of 2007, a law meant to protect rights, was later turned against the writer Shakthika Sathkumara, the social media commentator Ramzy Razeek and the comedian Natasha Edirisooriya. Sri Lanka doesn’t need to look abroad, or to speculate, to know what happens when broad powers are granted on the promise of narrow use.


Looking abroad, the clearest lessons I can find concern systems built first, with legal guardrails added late. Australia’s Robodebt scheme ran an automated debt-recovery algorithm against welfare recipients for years, and it was exposed only because there was a royal commission, a court and a free press, yet more than three years after the royal commission asked for a legal framework governing automated decisions, there still isn’t one. In India, Aadhaar enrolled more than a billion people before the Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right and limited the uses to which the identity system could be put, and the Unique Identification Authority now has a stated policy prohibiting the denial of essential services to anyone who lacks Aadhaar or fails authentication. Both show the courts and institutions doing remedial work after harm had already landed on the poorest and the least able to complain.

In each of these cases, harm arrived through ordinary administration, and fell first on those with the least power to contest it. Sri Lanka’s case is more dangerous still, because these instruments arrive together, are routed to a single office, the godlike Executive Presidency, and enter a country with a documented history of violently turning civic records against its own minorities.

Q: What meaningful safeguards should the Government secure before moving to implement such laws in the country?

A: Getting the sequence right matters more than anything else, so no further law should pass and no further database should connect until the PDPA is fully in force under an independent authority, including the rights to see, correct and erase personal data that the Government has left out of the January 2027 commencement. A data protection regime that arrives in 2027 to discipline systems built since 2023 comes years too late for anyone whose data is already in them. Parliament should also legislate only from a consolidated map of the whole architecture, covering every statute in force, every Bill and draft in circulation, the powers that overlap between them and what each agency may disclose to another, published in Sinhala, Tamil and English with clause-level rights and data protection assessments attached.

The single correction that would do most work across every one of these laws is to require a judge’s approval before any intrusion takes place. Every device search and data request, including the call, subscriber and location data a Deputy Inspector General can obtain under the POC Bill without one, should need a judicial order naming the account, device, dates and type of data sought. Independent reviewers should filter journalistic, legal, medical, survivor and research material out of what investigators ever see, the person affected should be told once an investigation no longer requires secrecy, and the state should publish annual figures on applications, approvals, refusals and urgent actions, which would compromise no investigation at all.

The triggers for these powers need narrowing. The POC Bill’s power to compel any provider of “locking or encryption services” to unlock what it holds should go, with partners saying plainly that they will not support measures that weaken encryption for everyone. The Online Safety Act’s false statement offence should be repealed now, rather than await a replacement that has yet to appear. The PSTA’s offence on information about police and military activity should be confined to genuinely secret material whose disclosure causes demonstrable harm, and both the PSTA and POC Bills need an express saving clause for journalism, research, satire, election observation, industrial action, protest and peaceful advocacy. 

Commissions and authorities regulating speech, association, finance or networks should be independent, appointed transparently, with fixed terms, technical qualifications and reporting to Parliament rather than to a Minister, defence and intelligence functions should sit outside civilian network security, and suspension, deregistration or the freezing of an organisation’s accounts should require a judicial order.

The World Bank, India, UNDP and the European Union should make an independent human rights impact assessment, trilingual publication and bars on function creep conditions of disbursement, with a standing power to pause finance when safeguards fail

Q: You are especially concerned that the Anti-Corruption Act and Proceeds of Crime Act, allows for access to a citizen’s financial records without his knowledge. How crucial a concern is this? And what safeguards do you believe should be in place before such laws are in place?

A: I want to be clear at the outset, since this is often misread, that nothing I’ve written argues against investigating corruption or recovering stolen assets, which this country badly needs, and the Anti-Corruption Act had strong civil society backing for good reason. Neither Act is an NGO surveillance law, and describing them that way would be wrong. My concern lies in what the two Acts authorise along the way, and in who else is swept up.

Both laws are already in force, the Anti-Corruption Act from 2023 and the Proceeds of Crime Act from 2025, so we are no longer discussing safeguards before they take effect but safeguards that are missing now. Between them, they permit covert surveillance, undercover operations, demands for telephone, banking, internet and traffic data from service providers, forced entry, the unlocking and decryption of devices, interception of communications and forensic extraction of data, in most cases with a judge’s approval obtained ex parte, which means without the person affected knowing or being heard. 

Under the Anti-Corruption Act, banks, the Inland Revenue Department and the Registrar of Companies must hand over account histories, transaction details and tax records on demand, telecommunications companies and internet providers can be required to hand over subscriber and usage data without a judicial warrant, section 59 lets authorities order any provider of encryption services to unlock or decrypt, and section 161 declares that the Act overrides any conflicting law. 

The Proceeds of Crime Act lets police demand passwords and force the unlocking of devices, defines a “document” to cover virtually any electronic data, and makes it a crime to tip someone off that they are under investigation. Late last year a police spokesperson confirmed on video that the police now have legal authority to tap phones, including WhatsApp, and to extract data forensically from seized handsets.

It matters a great deal, because financial investigation by its very nature maps relationships. Provider records, transfers and device contents reveal the sources, colleagues, donors, family members and partner organisations around whoever is under investigation, so a journalist’s confidential source can be identified from call records without anyone reading a single article, and people never suspected of anything find their privacy gone because they once sent money to, or called, someone who is. 

The safeguards needed are not complicated, starting with judicial authorisation resting on an objective connection between the offence, the property and the data sought, with orders naming accounts, devices, dates and data types rather than authorising open-ended collection. An independent reviewer should filter privileged journalistic, legal, medical and survivor material before investigators see it. The person affected should be notified once secrecy is no longer needed, and the state should publish annual figures on applications, approvals and refusals. The PDPA’s rights to see, correct and erase data should be in force, with purpose limits, retention rules and deletion after acquittal written into both Acts. And all of this depends on a judiciary that is independent of the executive, since a judge under pressure in a closed hearing is the only thing standing between a citizen and the state’s full view of their financial life.

Q: You expressed serious concerns that the draft’s failure to address input on AI-enabled surveillance and repression or discrimination and the algorithmic bias that would deepen it or more importantly the lack of accountability if and when the system failed a ‘performative consultation’?

A: Five working days were bad enough, though the consultation was performative above all because of what it was set up to hear. A document that would shape how AI enters tax, health, education, policing and public administration was put out in English alone, which guaranteed that the people most likely to be harmed would never read it, let alone respond, and its silences on surveillance, discrimination and redress were exactly the ones critical input would have exposed. Those omissions matter more now than they did in 2024, because a framework that ignores surveillance, bias and accountability at the outset is implemented without them, and the burden of retrofitting safeguards then falls on the people already harmed.

Later strategy documents have improved the presentation of rights, ethics and responsible AI, and I’ll acknowledge that, though as I said earlier, better vocabulary on its own changes nothing in practice. Meaningful safeguards change what the state may collect, who may query it, whether a person can refuse, and when a funder must stop paying, and on each of those questions the record remains thin. My study of Parliament’s debates found no match for human rights, ethical or child rights impact assessment across 173 Hansards.

 In February 2026, the Public Security Ministry described Police use of facial recognition and telephone-data analysis at Katunayake airport without any account of authorisation, accuracy, error rates, retention or how a mistaken identification could be challenged. The PDPA’s protection against automated decisions applies only to decisions made solely by a machine with an irreversible and continuous impact, which leaves out the far more common case of an official rubber-stamping an algorithm’s recommendation they may not understand.
